one_liner: Learning-project C++17 JSON DOM (shared_ptr nodes) that parses and walks 1.25-1.42x faster than nlohmann/json in its author's benchmark.
what_it_does: A DOM-only JSON library modeled on Java's org.json API. You build trees with JSONObject::put / JSONArray::put, parse a string or file into a JSONObject or JSONArray you pick in advance with JSONParser::parse (which returns a JSON_ERR_CODE and does not throw on malformed syntax), and serialize with toString(). Values come back through typed getters (getInt, getDouble, getString, getArray, getObject), which return 0, false, nullptr or an empty container on a missing key or a type mismatch. It is not a drop-in for nlohmann/json: there is no operator[], no set or erase, put() ignores a key that already exists, and there is no SAX, streaming or struct-mapping mode.
how_it_is_fast: Nothing exotic here. The parser is a hand-written, single-pass recursive-descent parser over a NUL-terminated char*. Objects are a flat std::vector<std::pair<std::string, shared_ptr>> searched by linear scan, and arrays are a std::vector<shared_ptr>. The author credits the read win to the 2026-09-22 switch to these vectors from the earlier unordered_map and list containers, while nlohmann/json stores objects in std::map by default. Serialization appends every node into one caller-owned buffer (appendTo). Each value is still its own make_shared heap node reached through virtual dispatch, which is why this was the slowest writer tested.
when_to_use: Reading small, trusted, machine-generated JSON: configs, or a few thousand records of plain ASCII strings, 32-bit ints and doubles, where you want error codes instead of exceptions and no dependencies
Projects that need public-domain (Unlicense) code, can vendor six .cpp files, and would otherwise use nlohmann/json only to parse and walk a DOM
Code ported from Java's org.json that should keep the same put/get shape in C++17
Learning or teaching how a shared_ptr/virtual-dispatch DOM compares with arena- and variant-based DOMs; the repo includes a harness comparing five libraries
when_not_to_use: Anything where speed matters beyond beating nlohmann/json. In the author's own tables, RapidJSON, simdjson (DOM) and glaze json_t read 2-7x faster. libJSON is also the slowest writer, e.g. 32,568.2 vs 21,225.0 us against nlohmann/json on 10,080 candles

Untrusted or arbitrary input. There is no conformance test suite and no nesting-depth limit in the recursive parser, bytes after the root value are not checked, and an integer outside 32-bit int makes std::stoi throw std::out_of_range even though the API reports errors by code

Anywhere you need a faithful round-trip. Doubles are written with std::to_string at six fixed decimals, so 1e-7 is written as 0.000000. Strings and keys are written without escaping, so a value that contains a quote or backslash produces invalid JSON
Editing documents in place. There is no public way to overwrite or remove a field, and put() silently keeps the old value; the author's own usability annex points this out
Objects with many keys. Each insert checks for a duplicate by linear scan and get() is linear, so building a large object costs O(n^2) and each lookup costs O(n)

integration.form: static lib (a shared build is optional via Conan -o shared=True / BUILD_SHARED_LIBS)
integration.dependencies: none for the library; GoogleTest (via Conan) only for tests. The documented build uses CMake >= 3.21 and Conan 2.x, but the six .cpp files can be vendored directly
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (the Conan recipe enforces cppstd 17); CMake 3.21+. No compiler versions are documented. Commit history targets Visual Studio 2017-2022, and the dev container uses GCC 12 on Debian 12
integration.platforms: any platform with a C++17 standard library (portable scalar code, no SIMD); only Windows/MSVC and Linux/GCC are evidenced in the repo
integration.thread_safety: not documented. The containers have no synchronization, and copies alias the same storage, so mutating through any copy while another thread reads is a data race

gotchas: Escape decoding is wrong: \n, \t, \r, \b and \f are stored as the plain letters n, t, r, b and f (JSONParser.cpp getStr). \uXXXX is decoded one code unit at a time, so UTF-16 surrogate pairs such as emoji are not combined, and the conversion uses std::wstring_convert, which has been deprecated since C++17
A number with an exponent but no fraction (1e5, 2E-3) is rejected with BAD_FORMAT_UNEXPECTED_VALUE, because the exponent is only parsed after a '.'
Copying a JSONObject or JSONArray shares its storage, which the author documents as a feature. Mutating a copy changes the original, and put(obj) stores a live handle rather than a snapshot

You must pick the root type before parsing (JSONObject or JSONArray), so a scalar or unknown-type root is unsupported. Parsing into a non-empty object appends to it, get() on a missing key allocates a fresh null node, and JSONArray::get(idx) has no bounds check
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose it over Boost.JSON, jsoncons or cJSON, which also beat nlohmann/json in their catalogued benchmarks (Boost.JSON by ~3.3-3.5x on citm_catalog parse), only if you specifically want Unlicense code with a Java org.json-style API and error codes, and your inputs are small and trusted. For speed, conformance or editing, glaze, simdjson or yyjson are better picks; the author says he would use glaze himself.
verified_claims_summary: The author's harness took the minimum of 30 sequential rounds in a CMake Release build with nlohmann/json 3.12.0 from Conan; compiler, flags and CPU are not stated. Parsing a random-walk OHLC document and walking the full DOM to sum open/high/low/close took libJSON 21.1 vs 26.4 us (10 candles), 2,632.2 vs 3,737.0 us (1,440) and 19,772.3 vs 27,254.9 us (10,080) against nlohmann/json. Caveat: each library parses its own writer's output. libJSON reads six-decimal doubles (about 10 characters each), while nlohmann/json reads its Grisu2 shortest-round-trip dump (about 17-18 characters for these values, roughly a third more bytes by my estimate), so part of the gap may come from input size rather than parser speed.
status_note: All recent activity is a one-day burst on 2026-09-22 (CMake/Conan build, GoogleTest, benchmarks, vector containers) after no commits since April 2024. It is Unlicense and only six .cpp files, so it is easy to vendor, but it is a self-described learning project with 0 stars, no CI and no external issues or PRs.
